name: Shechi: A Secure Distributed Computation Compiler Based on Multiparty Homomorphic Encryption
summary: A compiler for multiparty homomorphic encryption pipelines, written by the Sequre authors and built as a Codon extension: the artifact carries Codon IR helpers in C++ alongside 88 .codon files, 87 of whose paths it shares with Sequre. Codon is the substrate the whole system compiles through, and Shechi is the most recent work in the Codon lineage that extends the compiler rather than calling it.
why_codon: The work is a compiler built on Codon's IR, by the group that also wrote Sequre and co-authored the Codon paper.
note: The only work in the corpus citing four anchors. Has no paper DOI; six Zenodo artifact DOIs exist instead. Decor, curated later from the hand-collected set, states that it implemented its protocols in Shechi -- so Shechi now has a downstream user of its own inside this index, the same shape Sequre already had.

name: UniTe: A Universal Tensor Abstraction for Capturing Spatial Relationships
summary: An abstraction for spatial relationships between tensors defined against a common coordinate system, realised twice: as CoLa, a compression DSL built inside Codon, and as SHiM, a staged C++ DSL over BuildIt. The Codon half is a compiler modification, not a library -- CoLa's frontend is roughly 700 lines of Codon while its backend adds about 7,500 lines of C++ to Codon's own compiler, contributing view access propagation and location propagation passes. The paper also uses unmodified Codon as its baseline, reporting that CoLa as a pure library runs up to 65x slower than reference C before those passes, and reaches parity with the JPEG and H.264 reference implementations after them.
why_codon: The paper states CoLa implements UniTe within the Pythonic language Codon, that the authors modified Codon's compiler to add CoLa-specific transformation passes, and that unoptimized CoLa performance is equivalent to executing with Codon-proper.
note: Resolved from the full text under ruling 8, via an open copy in DSpace@MIT where the publisher page carries no PDF. First work found that both extends Codon and benchmarks against Codon-proper in the same evaluation. Jessica Ray is a co-author of the Codon paper.

name: An Empirical Study on the Performance and Energy Usage of Compiled Python Code
summary: A measurement study of what compiling Python actually buys, running seven benchmarks through eight tools -- PyPy, Numba, Nuitka, Mypyc, Codon, Cython, Pyston-lite and the experimental 3.13 build -- against CPython on two machines, recording energy, execution time and memory while varying CPU frequency and core count. Codon is one of the eight subjects, so the paper measures it rather than using or extending it, and it is the only work in the corpus that reports Codon's energy consumption as well as its speed.
why_codon: The paper states its subject is comparing the performance and energy efficiency of Python compilers, and names Codon among the eight it compiles with.
note: The natural companion to the repository-side benchmark entries. Where mce-sandbox and word-counter time Codon informally, this does it as a controlled study.

name: PopPy: Opportunistically Exploiting Parallelism in Python Compound AI Applications
summary: A system that finds parallelism in Python applications whose runtime is dominated by calls out to machine-learning models, on the argument that traditional optimizing compilers cannot help when execution time sits in external components. Codon is cited once, in the related-work paragraph on Python optimization, grouped with other systems that speed up bottleneck fragments of internal Python computation -- precisely the class of approach the paper argues is insufficient for compound AI workloads. Codon is never run.
why_codon: The full text cites Codon in a single related-work list of systems that optimize bottleneck fragments of Python, with no experiment involving it.
note: Resolved from the full text under ruling 8: the arXiv PDF has exactly one inline citation of the Codon reference, in the Python optimization paragraph of related work.

name: Pyls: Enabling Python Hardware Synthesis with Dynamic Polymorphism via LCRS Encoding
summary: A high-level synthesis framework that compiles dynamically polymorphic Python into monolithic hardware by representing every object as a Left-Child Right-Sibling tree, generating XLS IR and resolving types at runtime through a tree memory architecture, reporting large speedups over CPU and soft-core baselines on FPGA. Codon appears in the survey of approaches to Python performance, described there as compiling Python as a static language and using static type inference and cross-module optimisation to remove interpretation and dynamic dispatch overhead.
why_codon: The related-work section devotes a passage to Codon, quoting its claim to compile Python as a static language and describing its static type inference, compile-time optimisation and global optimisation across functions and modules. Codon is not part of the synthesis pipeline, which is XLS, and is not run.
note: Resolved from full text collected through an institutional login, after standing as the paper lane's first and longest-blocked work. The reading the abstract could not settle turns out to be the plain one. Worth noting what the two papers share: Pyls exists to bring dynamic polymorphism to Python hardware synthesis, and runtime polymorphism is one of the two limitations the Codon paper names for itself.
